motion: Does divine hiddenness make the existence of a perfectly loving God unlikely?

moves.sectionTitle: Perfect love and nonresistant nonbelief
moves.currentDescription: Perfect love directed toward relationship creates an expectation of accessible presence, making widespread exclusion of willing and able people surprising evidence against that divine profile.
moves.lockedProposition: A perfectly loving God who wants relationship with every willing and able person would not leave many such people without accessible experience of God.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: there are a few different ways to approach it but it's it's a fairly intuitive point that if there were a god who existed and particularly a god who loved us and wanted to enter into a relationship with anybody who was willing and able it seems surprising at the very least that so many people are restricted from experience of or with this god for so much of the time
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The move draws a direct probabilistic inference from perfect relational love to accessible divine presence, placing the observed exclusion of willing people squarely against the motion-level expectation. Principal limitation: Its evidence is primarily the intuitive fit between love and availability, without independently establishing how many excluded people are genuinely willing, able, and nonresistant or excluding morally sufficient reasons for temporary absence. Live burden: O'Connor must connect the general surprise to credible cases and show why individualized goods, temporal development, or human psychology cannot adequately explain restricted experience.

moves.sectionTitle: Perfect love and nonresistant nonbelief
moves.currentDescription: Natural theology may publicly support an inference to God without special revelation, so hiddenness must be weighed within total evidence rather than treated as evidentially decisive.
moves.lockedProposition: Hiddenness cannot by itself cancel the public evidence of natural theology, which may support an inference to God without special revelation.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: like on what grounds are we to believe that you know this one argument if you refer to to how schellenberg put it you know the divine the argument from divine hiddenness against god's existence in what sense are we to believe that the assertion or the perception of the skeptic or of someone like schellenberg that there isn't enough evidence for god kind of throws out all we know from natural theology and and does so objectively speaking so it seems like you have divine hiddenness as an argument on the one side and on the other side you have all the data you get or all the arguments you get from natural theology and it seems like on a very basic level that the argument as such seems to kind of claim that all of this needs to be put aside because natural theology as such is basically the claim that you know you you look at the world as it is you don't need special revelation and with the data you get you can make inference to the existence of god so i think that's one of the basic issues that uh that that you would want to look at when when they argue so the the the point being that the fact that there is this objection of the hiddenness of god doesn't necessarily outweigh all of those other
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Ruegger correctly identifies a cumulative-evidence requirement, reasoning that one adverse consideration cannot responsibly determine God's probability while cosmological or other natural-theological data remain relevant. Principal limitation: He neither specifies the arguments nor estimates their strength, and he initially treats hiddenness too much like a claim that all public evidence must be discarded rather than a prediction about loving personal accessibility. Live burden: The defense must show that evidence for a generic divine cause supports the specifically loving, relational God at issue and offsets the expected personal disclosure that O'Connor says is missing.

moves.sectionTitle: Perfect love and nonresistant nonbelief
moves.currentDescription: A genuinely willing nonbeliever supplies a counterinstance to universal divine openness, so even one such case requires a plausible explanation for continued non-disclosure.
moves.lockedProposition: A nonresistant nonbeliever desires relationship with God, and even one genuine instance requires the theist to supply a plausible reason for divine non-disclosure.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: non-resistant non-believer is the person who has no objection to entering into a relationship with god and in fact desires it and this would be someone that like like myself i think like if it's there i'm i'm here for it i really am i'm i'm open to it that is i'm non-resistant to this belief in god and so the reason we add that non-resistant clause is to say that is to prevent somebody from saying well maybe you're just sort of hardening your heart or something like this with as long as there is a single example just one of a truly non-resistant non-believer then it seems that the theist needs to explain why it is that god would hide his face from them or at least give us plausible reason to think that there could be such a reason yeah okay well
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: By defining nonresistance through willingness and desire for relationship, the move narrows the target and validly argues that one genuine counterinstance creates an explanatory burden for universal divine openness. Principal limitation: O'Connor's self-description supplies immediate testimony but not conclusive access to every relevant motive, while the inference also assumes that perfect love requires disclosure at the seeker's present time. Live burden: He must support the apparent genuineness of at least one case and answer defenses based on fallible introspection, changing resistance, delayed revelation, or unknown relational goods.

moves.sectionTitle: Perfect love and nonresistant nonbelief
moves.currentDescription: Even academically powerful arguments may fail to provide relational access, so their inability to bring willing seekers into belief preserves rather than answers hiddenness.
moves.lockedProposition: The hiddenness problem is not simply a shortage of arguments; it concerns why academically respectable evidence fails to bring willing people into belief and relationship.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: the divine hidden this problem i don't think i would characterize it as the problem that there sort of isn't enough evidence per se it's more something about the effect that that evidence has on the person who's considering belief so you know i think there's a great deal of of good evidence in terms of what is argumentatively sound um you know the fine-tuning argument you can make respond responses to it but yeah it's a powerful consideration why are the contents so finely tuned the argument from reason seems to be a powerful sort of undercutting uh reason to sort of distrust our our very reasoning faculties on atheism these kinds of things i think they are powerful argumentatively in a kind of academic sense they're they're easy to defend and difficult to argue against but of course particularly for christianity religion is not about natural theology natural theology is this this strange philosophical wart on the side of what is supposed to be this glorious relationship with a loving person i don't know if the natural
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: O'Connor grants that natural-theological arguments can be powerful, then precisely distinguishes academic defensibility from the belief-forming personal access predicted by Christianity's relational claims, directly answering Ruegger's cumulative-evidence framing. Principal limitation: The move does not yet establish that loving disclosure must produce belief in every willing subject, and its appeal to evidence's personal effect needs a clearer standard separating inadequate revelation from variable psychological uptake. Live burden: He must defend that standard against examples where good evidence fails to move people and show why natural theology cannot constitute an individualized route toward relationship.

moves.sectionTitle: Natural theology, personal revelation, and epistemic access
moves.currentDescription: A relational Christian God should be disclosed through accessible prayer, reflection, or experience, whereas technically demanding natural theology appears mismatched to the relationship being offered.
moves.lockedProposition: For a relational Christian God, prayer, reflection, or religious experience would be a more fitting and accessible disclosure than technically demanding natural theology.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: i were a christian i would think that this is not where i would expect to find the the the focal point of the christian faith this is supposed to be about a relationship i think look if if god has not revealed himself through through uh prayer or reflection or through religious experience it'd be very bizarre indeed for me to kind of put my eye down a microscope look at like a particular way that an atom wriggles or something you go out there he is you know it would be a very strange place for him to reveal himself and so i wouldn't expect so so when i say that sort of the natural theological arguments that they're argumentatively sound i think they are but they don't move me and i don't think they move a
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The move compares modes of disclosure and reasonably infers that prayer, reflection, or religious experience better fits a loving personal relationship than detecting an abstract cause through technical natural theology. Principal limitation: The fit judgment remains largely intuitive, and no evidence establishes that personal revelation must occur through O'Connor's preferred channels or that philosophical evidence cannot initiate relationship for differently constituted seekers. Live burden: He must justify a nonarbitrary threshold for accessible personal disclosure and explain why cumulative argument, practice, and gradual experience cannot jointly satisfy it.

moves.sectionTitle: Natural theology, personal revelation, and epistemic access
moves.currentDescription: Sound evidence sometimes fails to produce corresponding conduct because psychology intervenes, so a seeker's unchanged response does not alone demonstrate inadequate evidence or disclosure.
moves.lockedProposition: Evidence can be adequate even when human psychology prevents it from producing action, as familiar cases such as smoking illustrate.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: i guess then we're really talking about well you know some a person like yourself looking at the evidence and i think that the crucial turn there is it doesn't move you so what do you i mean could you kind of mention another example where where the evidence moves you to you know to action or to to whatever it supposes it's supposed to do to move you towards because i feel like you know i can look at i don't know i can look at any piece of evidence about anything i don't know about you know trees or transportation whatever and not be moved by it the question is well why should a piece of data or like a body of data move me to anything i'm not trying to kind of to trick you or to undermine you in any in any sense but just trying to understand what do you understand under this term that that evidence should move you because that's like the way i see it is that while you're presented with evidence and if something makes sense to you then the most reasonable thing is for you to act in accordance with it i mean take the example of smoking i mean it's it's quite out of question that smoking damages your health so that means that well people should be moved to not smoke but that's not what what happened so that the question is or it seems to me that the problem is not with the evidence as such which can or cannot move people to do something or to act in a certain way so what what is this moving except what do you think i mean i'm
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Ruegger identifies the legitimate distinction between evidence quality and psychological uptake, using smoking to demonstrate concretely that acknowledged reasons do not invariably control a person's response. Principal limitation: The analogy shifts from involuntary belief acquisition and relational awareness to voluntary conduct, so it contacts O'Connor's word “move” without establishing that available divine evidence is adequate for forming belief. Live burden: Ruegger must separate belief, emotion, and action, then provide a better-matched account showing how sufficient personal disclosure could leave a genuinely willing seeker unable to assent.

moves.sectionTitle: Natural theology, personal revelation, and epistemic access
moves.currentDescription: Conviction arises involuntarily when accepted premises and valid inference compel assent, defeating analogies that equate failing to believe with choosing not to act.
moves.lockedProposition: A person cannot simply choose belief; conviction occurs involuntarily when an argument's premises and inference actually compel assent.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: just curious there are some arguments that i have experienced that have sort of moved me to change my beliefs and it happens essentially non-consensually this is the weird thing about becoming convinced of an argument it just sort of happens to you right and so so for example when i first started considering arguments surrounding free will when i was like 17 or something and i never really thought about it and you know i listened to the audiobook of sam harris's book about free will and i'm just kind of staring off into space like this is incredible and and that seemed to have an effect and i think that the reason has got something to do with maybe if you can present a sort of valid syllogism a deductive argument in which i sort of believe the premises then i have no choice but to believe the conclusion and so natural theology has a
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: O'Connor directly defeats the smoking comparison by distinguishing chosen conduct from nonconsensual conviction and explaining how accepted premises plus valid inference can compel a conclusion without a further decision. Principal limitation: His autobiographical example supports the phenomenology of sudden persuasion but does not prove that every belief is wholly involuntary or identify which missing premise prevents natural theology from compelling him. Live burden: He must connect doxastic involuntarism to divine responsibility, showing why a loving God should supply belief-forming grounds rather than merely leave seekers with arguments they can continue evaluating.

moves.sectionTitle: Temporal disclosure, salvation, and scriptural consistency
moves.currentDescription: Revising one's assessment after understanding an argument is ordinary intellectual correction, so O'Connor's changed appraisal does not demonstrate gradual personal revelation by God.
moves.lockedProposition: Coming to understand and admire an argument is ordinary intellectual correction, not evidence of personal divine revelation.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: okay a lot of people have said to me look you you really need to revisit this so i do and i look at it and i think wow this is actually quite interesting this is this is quite this is quite powerful i wouldn't say that sort of god has come out from hiding here this is an example of me misunder misunderstanding an argument and then upon understanding it thinking that it's very clever and i don't think my view on on how good it is has changed since then
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: O'Connor offers a parsimonious rival explanation of his changed appraisal, distinguishing correction of a misunderstood argument from the much stronger claim that God personally emerged from hiddenness. Principal limitation: The reply establishes that ordinary learning can explain the change, but it cannot exclude the possibility that such learning also participates in a broader sequence of disclosure. Live burden: He must specify what additional feature would distinguish personal revelation from intellectual improvement and show why Ruegger's longitudinal interpretation lacks independent support beyond compatibility with theism.

moves.sectionTitle: Temporal disclosure, salvation, and scriptural consistency
moves.currentDescription: Present felt absence may be only a temporal snapshot, since divine disclosure and relationship could deepen across a longer personal process not yet completed.
moves.lockedProposition: A present snapshot of felt absence may not establish permanent divine hiddenness because disclosure and relationship may deepen over time.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: not revealing himself yet i think and i've mentioned this like previous to our conversation i think there is a kind of a snapshot and frame of reverence reference you can take when talking about this problem of hiddenness which i by which i mean you know how do i feel about god or how do i think about god today on this 11th of july in 2022 and it seems to me you know someone might say well god is hidden well i can't experience him again both the christian or the non-christian may actually have that sort of sentiment or feeling but then another way to look at the whole issue is well you look at the period of time and well how has has god been revealing himself to me or have i experienced some sort of increased relationship or increased depth of relationship with god and here is
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Ruegger exposes a temporal assumption in moving from present absence to permanent hiddenness, offering a coherent possibility that disclosure and relationship develop across a seeker's longer history. Principal limitation: Possibility alone supplies little evidence that such a process is occurring, will conclude, or remains compatible with perfect love when sincere seeking persists without recognizable personal contact. Live burden: He must identify indicators of gradual disclosure, address cases interrupted by death, and explain why delay produces goods unavailable through earlier modest revelation.

moves.sectionTitle: Temporal disclosure, salvation, and scriptural consistency
moves.currentDescription: If later belief is necessary for salvation, permitting current nonbelief risks profound unfairness because death may interrupt the proposed journey before disclosure ever arrives.
moves.lockedProposition: If salvation requires later belief, permitting present nonbelief as part of a delayed journey risks grave unfairness when death interrupts that journey.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: maybe god just has good reason to sort of allow me to be mistaken so that then in the future i become sort of a theist and then maybe it's something to do with that journey that actually sort of shows people that you know if they're experiencing doubts that maybe that this is something that that happens to people but then there are all kinds of problems that are raised by that um for example the problem of believing in libertarian free will as a theist if you think if you're the kind of theist that thinks that sort of my acceptance of the sacrifice of jesus is somehow necessary to my salvation then as long as you believe that there are sort of free human beings who are actually able to do what they like then sure maybe god has some grand plan whereby you know i i'm not a theist and then 10 years in the future i become a theist and this has some great sort of practical import but maybe like four years into that somebody sort of freely chooses to come and murder me somebody hits me with their car or something like that and so i never actually make it that far this seems to be a bit of a problem here for me which is that well if the reason why i wasn't the theist at the moment of my death was because god was doing something himself was like sort of purposefully trying to enact this plan where i eventually become a theist one day but this gets interrupted because of the existence of free will and so i end up going to go into the afterlife not saved that seems incredibly unfair
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The move tests temporal disclosure against its highest practical stakes, inferring that a delayed path becomes morally precarious if death can prevent the later belief required for salvation. Principal limitation: The argument is conditional upon a particular relationship between explicit belief and salvation, while the exchange does not establish Ruegger's complete soteriology or exclude postmortem and nonbelief-compatible possibilities. Live burden: O'Connor must secure the salvation premise and demonstrate that interruption is not merely conceivable but a genuine problem for the defended Christian account.

moves.sectionTitle: Temporal disclosure, salvation, and scriptural consistency
moves.currentDescription: O'Connor's shift from dismissing to admiring an argument could indicate gradual disclosure, suggesting that divine access is developing rather than remaining wholly absent.
moves.lockedProposition: Alex's movement from dismissing to admiring an argument may be evidence that disclosure is occurring gradually rather than being wholly absent.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Ruegger applies the temporal defense to concrete biographical evidence, proposing that O'Connor's movement from dismissal to admiration may represent an early stage of disclosure rather than static absence. Principal limitation: The inference moves too quickly from intellectual reassessment to divine action, since ordinary correction explains the same evidence without establishing personal contact, divine agency, or movement toward Christian belief. Live burden: He must provide a discriminator between gradual revelation and normal philosophical learning and show why admiration of one argument materially answers relational hiddenness.

moves.sectionTitle: Temporal disclosure, salvation, and scriptural consistency
moves.currentDescription: Claiming that everyone already has sufficient evidence conflicts with saying God intentionally delays disclosure, because withholding appears unnecessary once adequate access has supposedly been provided.
moves.lockedProposition: The defense cannot coherently claim both that everyone already has sufficient evidence and that God withholds disclosure for good reasons.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: i i understand that this could be a this could be an argument this could be it could be like well look yeah i know that that you don't feel god's presence i know that he's not making himself known to you but he's doing that on purpose it seems strange to me to put that in the same argument or in the same position against this problem as saying that but look there is all of this evidence there is all of this natural theology that you're sort of ignoring or not understanding or rejecting but then also saying that actually no the reason that you don't feel god is because god has good reason to sort of hide himself from you these seem to rub up against each other as well as of course the scripture seems to be littered with references to the idea that people should be able to believe in god you know the fall in his heart says there is no god romans 1 is a famous example of people saying that this is god saying that essentially the evidence that's been provided to everybody is such that they are without excuse for not having belief in him i i'm i don't mind somebody saying yeah that's what romans 1 means and it's correct that there is enough evidence for everybody and you're just somehow missing it or ignoring it or something or somebody saying you know that there actually isn't enough evidence that's been provided to you and god has good reason for that but i don't think you can do both at once
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: O'Connor identifies a structural tension between claiming universally sufficient evidence and explaining hiddenness through purposeful withholding, since adequate disclosure appears already achieved under the first claim but absent under the second. Principal limitation: The tension is not a strict contradiction if sufficient propositional evidence and delayed experiential or relational disclosure are distinguished, or if people receive different evidential forms over time. Live burden: He must show that Ruegger used “enough” in the same belief-forming sense contested by hiddenness and prevent the defense from separating generic theistic warrant from fuller personal revelation.

moves.sectionTitle: Resistance, self-knowledge, and changing attitudes
moves.currentDescription: Sustained engagement with Christians, scripture, theology, and Bible study makes O'Connor presently apparently nonresistant, regardless of any earlier anti-theistic posture or unwillingness.
moves.lockedProposition: Whatever his earlier posture, Alex's present sustained engagement with Christians, scripture, theology, and Bible study makes him apparently nonresistant by any reasonable standard.

Live burden: He must defend the threshold as sufficient for nonresistance while acknowledging introspective limits and separating reasonable openness from an impossible demand for demonstrable motivational purity.

moves.sectionTitle: Resistance, self-knowledge, and changing attitudes
moves.currentDescription: O'Connor's movement from anti-theistic unwillingness toward openness shows that resistance changes over time and may partly arise from a seeker's own developing posture.
moves.lockedProposition: Alex's movement from anti-theistic unwillingness to willingness shows that resistance can change and may partly belong to the seeker's own posture.

Live burden: Ruegger must connect the historical change to ongoing hiddenness, demonstrate that relevant resistance persists now, or explain why disclosure may reasonably lag after the seeker becomes willing.

moves.sectionTitle: Resistance, self-knowledge, and changing attitudes
moves.currentDescription: Although hidden resistance remains logically possible, that possibility supplies no evidence that an apparently sincere and open seeker is actually resisting divine relationship.
moves.lockedProposition: Hidden resistance is logically possible, but invoking that possibility does not establish that an apparently open seeker is actually resistant.

Principal limitation: Limited self-knowledge does not provide affirmative evidence of resistance, so the move weakens certainty about a case without explaining why a loving God remains inaccessible to an apparently sincere seeker. moves.sectionTitle: Resistance, self-knowledge, and changing attitudes
moves.currentDescription: Some people resist divine authority or religious lifestyle costs, but those genuine motivational cases do not justify concluding that the same explanation applies to O'Connor.
moves.lockedProposition: Some nonbelief is genuinely motivated by resistance to divine authority or lifestyle costs, though Lukas declines to infer that this explains Alex.

Live burden: He must show that resistance explains all relevant counterexamples or supply an independent reason why perfect love permits hiddenness for seekers whose motives provide no such explanation.

moves.sectionTitle: Belief, relationship, trust, and practical cost
moves.currentDescription: Requiring major Christianity-specific lifestyle costs before adequate grounds for belief reverses reasonable trust, making prescribed practice an unfair gateway to recognizing Christianity as true.
moves.lockedProposition: A seeker cannot reasonably be required to bear major Christianity-specific lifestyle costs before receiving adequate grounds for believing Christianity true.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: O'Connor links epistemic order to practical stakes, arguing that substantial Christianity-specific sacrifices reasonably require prior grounds for believing the authority and relationship that allegedly justify them. Principal limitation: The inference assumes that exploratory practice entails major commitment and cannot itself generate legitimate evidence, while some low-cost forms of participation might precede settled belief without reversing reasonable trust. Live burden: He must distinguish permissible investigation from identity-altering sacrifice and show why Ruegger's proposed gateway demands the latter before adequate confirmation.

moves.sectionTitle: Belief, relationship, trust, and practical cost
moves.currentDescription: Religious practice and provisional acceptance may initiate relationship with God before settled propositional belief, reversing the assumption that conviction must always precede relational participation.
moves.lockedProposition: Religious practice and acceptance may initiate a relationship with God even before the agnostic acquires propositional belief.

moves.lockedProposition: Belief-free 'relationship' is too indeterminate and costly when the alleged partner supplies no accessible confirmation of being in the relationship.

moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Ruegger candidly presents a bounded possibility that costly trust may precede experiential disclosure for some people, directly confronting rather than evading O'Connor's objection about epistemic order. Live burden: He must identify a relational good uniquely secured by the leap and explain how seekers can distinguish warranted trust from arbitrary commitment or psychologically manufactured confirmation.
